To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
HIV-infected men (vs. women) had a higher prevalence of coronary atherosclerosic plaque and high-risk plaque morphology.

ART-treated HIV-positive women had a lower burden of coronary plaque and high risk coronary plaque morphology than ART-treated HIV-positive men, and that male sex remained an independent correlate of coronary plaque burden and high risk coronary morphology in this population.
ART-treated HIV+ women (vs. ART-treated HIV+ men) had a 2.4-fold lower prevalence of any coronary plaque and a 3.1-fold lower prevalence of high risk positively remodeled plaque.
In summary, our research is concerned with
sex differences in subclinical coronary atheroma burden among HIV-infected individuals receiving antiretrovirus therapy.
understanding the mechanisms underlying cardiovascular disease in people with HIV.
the mechanisms that drive sex differences in cardiovascular risk among people living with HIV.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
HIV-infected men have higher prevalence of subclinical atherosclerosis than HIV-infected women.
HIV-infected men have more coronary atherosclerotc plaque than HIV-infected women.
HIV infected women on ART had less subclinical coronary plaque compared to HIV infected men on ART, but the mechanisms of this difference remain to be elucidated.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
HIV-infected men have higher burden and higher prevalence of coronary plaque than women, and this is independent of the cardiovascular risk factors.
ART-treated HIV infection is associated with subclinical coronary plaque, and this association is more pronounced in HIV-infected men compared with HIV-infeted women.
HIV-infected men and women on ART have a higher risk of cardiovascular disease (CVD) than the general population and the risk is higher in women.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the sex differences we observed in subclinical coronary atheroma are unlikely to explain sex differences in the incidence of MI in HIV-infected persons.
the higher risk of MI among HIV-infected women compared to HIV-infected men may reflect sex-specific mechanisms beyond coronary atherosclerosis.
HIV-infected men have more subclinical coronary plaque than HIV-infected women.
